about: Every defect found in this repository from inside it, with the mechanism that found it and the test that keeps it found. This file is data: scripts/figures.py counts it and checks that every test named here is one pytest actually collects, so the number in the README cannot drift from the repository the way a typed figure does. Two entries are not defects in the shipped tool and say so: one was the eval measuring the cost of a policy, one was a defect in the measuring apparatus. They are here because they were found the same way everything else was. At 3.0.0 the model-scanner was archived; the defects it recorded stay here, with `pinned_note` naming the test file that pinned each one at tag v2.3.0, because a defect deleted from the ledger is a defect nobody can learn from.

found_by_meanings.test suite: a test that was written for something else failed
found_by_meanings.adversarial engineering review: the code read as an attacker would read it, looking for the call that never happens
found_by_meanings.adversarial legal review: the governance catalogue read against the Official Journal
found_by_meanings.fuzzing: coverage-guided mutation over every parser, deterministic seeds
found_by_meanings.benign corpus: the half of the eval corpus that must not fail
found_by_meanings.real-serialiser corpus: artifacts written by torch, safetensors, onnx and h5py rather than crafted
found_by_meanings.benchmark self-tests: the tests that check the comparison is fair to the other tools
found_by_meanings.exhaustive sweep: every input in a bounded space, not a sample
found_by_meanings.reading the tool's own output: running it on a real artifact and looking at what came back
found_by_meanings.running the harness: a figure the harness printed that could not be true
found_by_meanings.external adversarial audit: the repository read by someone outside it, looking for the claim the code does not check
found_by_meanings.running the gate: `make lint`, `make test` or `make fuzz` refused the working tree
found_by_meanings.product review against a roadmap: the repository read against a written plan for what it should become, looking for the place the plan's first requirement was already violated
found_by_meanings.writing a test for an adjacent feature: a test written for something new asserted, for the first time, on a value the old code had always produced incorrectly
found_by_meanings.adversarial review of new code: the modules written for this release read back as an attacker would read them, before the release, looking for the path the tests were written around
found_by_meanings.using the tool as a person would: the commands run end to end against a workspace written the way somebody would write it, rather than the way the fixtures do
found_by_meanings.running it on the runner for the first t: the published integration executed where it actually runs, on a GitHub Actions runner. `make all` on a clean clone deliberately reaches none of it - there is no runner on a laptop - so this is the one mechanism in the list that costs a push to operate
found_by_meanings.an intermittent failure on one interpret: a test that passes almost always failed on one of the three interpreters in a run where the other two passed, so the difference was timing rather than code. It is the kind of red build that gets re-run rather than read, which is why the mechanism is named: the re-run is the bug's best defence
found_by_meanings.reading the vendor's documentation: the vendor's own reference read against what this tree does with the key it documents, rather than the tree read against itself. The mechanism is named because two greps of our own constants came back short before it was used: a set of values is a fact about somebody else's software, and a grep of our code can only ever return what we already knew.
found_by_meanings.running the gate on the development mach: the suite run on Windows, where the tree is written, rather than in WSL, where the gate runs. Named because the two are not the same machine and rule 7 of CLAUDE.md puts the gate in WSL on purpose: anything only Windows sees is outside what the gate measures, which makes it invisible rather than absent.

defects.title: Trailing zero padding was passed over in silence
defects.effect: Padding after the final STOP never reaches the unpickler, so failing on it would be noise, but saying nothing made the report read as though the whole file had been analysed.

defects.effect: The catalogue's "what Actaira provides" lines were printed under the word provides for every applicable obligation, evidence or none, so a run that established nothing read like a run that had.

defects.title: The concatenated-stream budget failed open
defects.effect: The walker stops after eight trailing streams and simply left the loop: no finding, `truncated` never set, `fully_read` still True. A legacy magic number to suppress the concatenation finding, eight one-byte fillers to exhaust the budget and a gadget as stream nine gave a 115-byte file an empty findings list, max_severity None, PASS and exit 0 under both policies, while any consumer that loads more than one object from the stream runs os.system.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_formats.py, test_fuzz_regressions.py`

defects.title: A MARK-built tuple kept only its last element
defects.effect: `stack_before` is listed bottom to top, and the walk read every entry as if it sat above the mark: it popped one slice item as a fixed operand, never popped the container below the mark, and discarded the rest of the slice. TUPLE, which is what a pickler emits for more than three arguments, produced a one-element tuple holding the last argument, so a payload handed to a nested loader in any position but the last was invisible to the nested-loader check.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_formats.py`

defects.title: GLOBAL's module and name were split from the left
defects.effect: `pickletools` renders GLOBAL's two newline-terminated fields joined by a space, so a module name containing a space had its first token read as the module and everything after it as the callable. Not exploitable, because such a module cannot be imported, and fixed because a scanner that reports a callable the file does not name is wrong in the direction that matters least until the day it is not.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_pickle_scan.py`

defects.title: INST imported a callable and was never judged
defects.effect:
INST carries module and name inline exactly as GLOBAL does and reaches find_class at load time exactly as GLOBAL does, but it lived only in EXECUTION_OPCODES, where it was counted and never passed to the policy. Twenty-seven bytes of protocol 0, (S'echo PWNED'
ios
system
., ran a denylisted callable and passed under both policies with one INFO line. The design note at the top of the module enumerates the import primitives and forgot this one.

defects.title: A tail the walker could not measure was dropped in silence
defects.effect: Real pickle reads I\\x00\\n. as the integer 0 followed by STOP where pickletools raises on it, so the trailing-stream walker could not compute the stream's length and returned, while the parse error that would have shown it was suppressed by the torch legacy exemption. A 48-byte file with an os.system gadget behind that divergence reached PASS with exit 0, and a repeated-load consumer ran it. The exemption is now bounded to the storage region, whose position is measured from a checkpoint torch wrote.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_formats.py`

defects.title: An RFC 3161 token whose signature was never checked read as a verified one
defects.effect: `signature_state: not_verified` - no certificate in the token, an algorithm this verifier does not implement, or anything the two broad `except` clauses in `_check_signature` swallowed - was accepted by `ok` exactly as `embedded_cert_only` was. The one field a caller looks at could not tell a checked token from an unchecked one, in a module whose docstring ends "Never say verified about something that was not".

defects.title: manifest.tsr was covered by no signature at all
defects.effect: The token cannot appear in `files` - it is issued over the manifest's pending form - and that was read as "cannot be covered", so it sat outside the file list and outside the Ed25519 signature. The only cross-checks were the genTime and the serial the manifest advertises, both of which a second token minted with the same values satisfies, and Actaira verifies no TSA chain. Swapping the token needed no key and left every check green.

defects.title: --extends returned before verification, so every trust flag was ignored in silence
defects.effect: `actaira verify NEW --extends OLD` ran the consistency proof and returned, never reaching `verify_package`. `--require-trust` and `--trusted-keyring` were parsed, accepted and discarded: a package signed by a key the caller had explicitly said they did not accept exited 0.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_cli.py`

defects.title: A trust anchor that would not load was indistinguishable from no anchor
defects.effect: A keyring with `key` for `keys`, a `keys` that was a string, an empty `keys`, or `--pubkey ""` all produced an empty anchor set, which fell through to the `embedded_key_only` branch: OK, exit 0, and the caller's assertion about whose signatures they accept dropped without a word - along with every revocation that keyring carried. An unparseable `--pubkey` propagated a ValueError out of the verifier instead.

defects.title: A manifest claiming rfc3161 with no timestamp block compared every field with itself
defects.effect: `declared.get("gen_time") not in (None, actual)` and `str(declared.get("serial_number", actual)) != str(actual)` both pass when the block is absent, and `timestamp_subject` strips the block so removing it does not change what the TSA signed. A token issued in 1999 over the right digest verified and was reported as third-party time evidence.

defects.title: The no-score guard read keys and never values
defects.effect: The guard on the governance layer's thesis walked dictionary keys only, and only through dicts and lists. "Actaira rates this obligation 87% compliant (grade B, overall score 4.2/5)" in `governance.AIA-4.summary` left all 172 governance tests green while every rendering printed a grade. It also missed an integer under a neutral key (`readiness_index: 87`), stepped over tuples, and was applied to the assessment dictionary alone - not to `governance clock --json`, the text renders, the dossier, the catalogues or the web routes.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_governance.py`

defects.title: The dossier's subject digest was written and never read
defects.effect: `governance/pack.py` files the dossier under the digest of the artifact set it covers and repeats that set as `subjects`; nothing in `attest/` read either. The naive forgery breaks `prev_hash` and was caught, but re-linking - appending the stolen dossier through `chain.append` onto another package's inspections - recomputes every link, the Merkle root, the head and the signature, and verified clean with the assessment now sitting at the end of a chain it was never computed from.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_governance.py`

defects.title: The fuzzer published its argument as a measurement
defects.effect: `"iters": config.iters` is the number on the command line. The worker had always written the real count to `state/worker.json` and nobody read it, and `except Exception: break` on a worker that died without leaving state finished the run silently - so a run that executed twelve cases published the full figure, zero findings and exit 0, and `scripts/figures.py` summed those figures into the README.

defects.title: A control character in a member name destroyed the whole JUnit report
defects.effect: XML 1.0 cannot represent a C0 control, escaped or otherwise. `ElementTree` wrote the byte out and every parser then rejected the document, so one member called `weights\u0001.bin` inside one artifact cost the entire report rather than one line of it - and a runner shows a report it cannot parse as no tests at all, which is the silent pass the three-verdict mapping exists to prevent.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went with the module it covered in phase A, which removed everything no command could reach; it is at commit e13b1bc, `tests/test_junit.py`

defects.title: Every ML-BOM was invalid against the CycloneDX version it declared
defects.effect: `modelCard.modelParameters` is declared with `additionalProperties: false` and a closed field list, and this emitted a `properties` array inside it. Tools that do not validate accepted the document, which is why it shipped; tools that do rejected all of it. Separately, `bom-ref` was derived from the digest alone, so one document covering the same bytes twice - a file and a copy of it in one directory - carried two components under one reference.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_bom.py`

defects.title: Four limits the local server did not have, and one set on the wrong object
defects.effect: `verify_package` read every package member with `ZipFile.read`, which decompresses without limit, so a 1.4 MiB package posted to `/api/verify` allocated gigabytes. A multipart part could carry unbounded headers and a request unbounded parts and field names, each capped individually and never counted. And `_Server.timeout` was read by `handle_request()`, which `serve_forever()` never calls, so the slowloris bound it was written for did not exist. Neither `Origin` nor `Host` was checked, leaving CSRF through the operator's browser and DNS rebinding open.
defects.pinned_note: the test that pinned this went to archive/model-scanner with the module it covered; it is at tag v2.3.0, `tests/test_web_limits.py`

defects.title: safety_results.json was tracked and rewritten by every benchmark run
defects.effect: fickling appends its scan output to it on each `make benchmark`, so a benchmark run produced a 300 KB diff of another tool's output on top of the previous run's. Reviewing it told a reader nothing, and it was the only run artifact in the repository that was not ignored.
defects.not_shipped_because: repository hygiene, not a fault in the tool

defects.title: The read bounded to protect memory allocated its whole ceiling for every file
defects.effect: `io_budget.read_at_most` called `handle.read(limit + 1)`. That is correct, and CPython allocates the requested size up front and then shrinks the object to what it actually read - so every pickle asked the allocator for 512 MiB before reading its bytes, a 16-byte one exactly as much as a real checkpoint, and every GGUF header asked for 64 MiB. On Linux the allocation is lazy and the pages are never touched, which is why this lived through five releases and a CI job that only ever ran on Linux. On a platform that commits what it allocates it costs about 78 ms per artifact and a real 512 MiB spike: `make benchmark` on Windows measured a median of 66 ms per file where the recorded Linux run of the same corpus measured 0.175 ms, and a scan of the 64-artifact corpus spent four and a half seconds in the allocator. The module's own docstring is what makes this more than a slow path - it exists so that 'a file that makes the auditor run out of memory is a file that does not get audited' cannot happen, and the bound it introduced was allocating the ceiling for every file regardless of size. The budget is a decision about the format; the allocation is now a fact about the file, from `os.fstat` on the already-open handle so there is no window in which the file could be replaced between the two. Median per artifact went from 70.0 ms to 0.568 ms on the machine that found it. Found by running `make benchmark` with the real rival tools on a platform the project had never measured on.

defects.title: `watch` measured a local artifact's digest, compared against it, and then stored neither the digest nor any evidence about it
defects.effect: The filesystem connector publishes no `declared_sha256` by design (D-85b): a digest this tool computed and then compared against itself is not a check, so the field stays empty and `measured_sha256` carries what was actually read. `_write` and `_record_evidence` both consulted `declared_sha256` alone. The consequence on a local source, which is the commonest workspace there is, was that every artifact asset row was stored with an empty `digest` column and no per-artifact evidence record was written at all - while the same run used the measured digest to correctly report CONTENT_DRIFT. The measurement existed and was discarded one line before it was written down. Everything downstream reads that column: supersession is bound to a subject's digest (D-223), so there was nothing to supersede and a changed model invalidated nothing; `state.record.resolve` finds a scanned file by its digest, so no scan could ever be filed against a locally observed artifact; and the graph panel showed a digest-less node. The fix is one helper, `watch.artifact_digest`, that returns the strongest digest a snapshot holds - measured before declared - together with the basis it came from, so the two claims stay distinguishable in the asset attributes and in the evidence payload rather than being merged into one field that reads as identity.

defects.title: DEF-74's fix has never worked on Windows, because a URI was parsed with a string slice
defects.effect: `snapshot._measure` turned a `file:` URI into a path with `uri[len('file://'):]`. On POSIX that is right by coincidence. On Windows `file:///C:/models/w.bin` becomes `/C:/models/w.bin`, which is not a path that exists, so `is_file()` was false, `_measure` returned an empty string, and no local artifact was ever measured. Comparison then fell back to size - which is precisely the DEF-74 failure DEF-74 exists to prevent: a weight file replaced with different bytes of the same length comes back UNCHANGED, exit 0. It also mishandled percent-escapes on every platform, so a directory with a space in its name was never measured either. The regression test written for DEF-74 did not catch any of it, because its fixture assembled `file://` plus a native path by hand and that spelling is the one shape the old slice happened to survive; the connector emits `Path.as_uri()`, which it did not. The fix is `urllib.request.url2pathname`, which is per-platform by construction, with the hand-assembled spelling still accepted so that a URI written by a person does not silently fall back to a byte count. The fixture now uses the spelling the connector actually produces.

defects.title: every receipt ever issued from a workspace referenced no evidence, because nothing is filed under a subject handle
defects.effect: `assurance-receipt/v2` publishes an `evidence` array so that a receipt can name the observations it rested on, and `receipt issue --state` gathered it by matching each stored record's `subject_id` against the subject's handle - `artifact:model.pkl` - and against `claims.subject`, which for an artifact is its digest. No evidence is ever filed under either. `watch` files per-artifact records under an id derived from the artifact's URI, and the producers added in 2.3.0 file scans, assessments and decisions under that same id, so the two sets never intersected and the array was empty in every receipt ever issued from a workspace. The command exited 0 and wrote a valid signed document each time, which is what made it invisible: the field a verifier would read to learn which observations the receipt rested on was simply absent, and absence is indistinguishable from a workspace that had recorded nothing. This is the third time this exact shape has been found in this repository, after the `decisions` and `receipts` tables in D-233: a published contract field with no producer that could populate it. The fix routes the lookup through `state.record.resolve`, which is the function the producers themselves use to answer 'which recorded asset is this subject', so the two ends agree by construction rather than by two similar-looking expressions staying equal.

defects.title: the workflow invoked zizmor as `python -m zizmor`, which is not a thing
defects.effect: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installed `zizmor` and then ran `python -m zizmor`. zizmor is a Rust binary distributed through PyPI: `pip install` puts an executable on PATH and ships no importable module, so the step died with `No module named zizmor` on its first execution. It had never been executed before - every local run during phase S3 called the binary by its path in a venv, which is the one spelling the workflow does not use, so the clean zizmor output quoted in the phase commit was real and was obtained a different way from the one the gate would use. The fix is to call `zizmor` and to PIN it to 1.30.1: an unpinned linter turns this job red on somebody else's release, and a gate that goes red for a reason that is not a change to this repository is one people learn to skip.
defects.found_by: running it on the runner for the first time
defects.pinned_note: NOT REPRODUCIBLE WITH A STUB, and this entry names the run instead rather than pretending otherwise. The fact that broke is a property of a third-party distribution - that it has no importable module - and the only place it can be observed is where that distribution is installed. Installing zizmor in the suite would make it a test dependency of a tool whose whole argument is that it has one runtime dependency, and it is deliberately installed in its own CI job and nowhere else; a stub that emulated `pip` and a missing module would be a test of Python's `-m` semantics rather than of this repository. The regression test is the `workflows` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which runs on every push. It first failed in run 35381167282 and first passed in run 35382239038.

defects.title: the Action's exit code was unreadable in the only case it matters, because a failed composite maps no outputs
defects.effect: `action.yml` published an `exit-code` output and this repository's own CI job read it. A composite action whose step fails does not map its outputs, so the value was an empty string exactly when a rule had fired - the clean run reported `0` and the keyv run reported nothing. The job compared an empty string against `1` and failed, which is the lucky direction; written a little more loosely it would have compared two empty strings and passed. It is also a false promise in published metadata, which is the class this phase built `readme_claims_resolve_against_the_tree` for and which that check cannot see because it reads pages and not `action.yml`. The fix writes the number to `actaira-exit-code.txt` before anything can fail, moves the failing into a step of its own so the step that records the outputs succeeds, and says in the output's own description that a caller who needs it on failure reads the file.
defects.found_by: running it on the runner for the first time
defects.pinned_note: The two tests pin the REMEDY and not GitHub's behaviour: they execute the step bodies and require the exit code to be recorded in a file and in `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` whatever the tool exited with, and the pass-through step to exit with that number. Remove the file write and they fail. That a failed composite maps no outputs is a fact about the runner and no stub can show it; it was observed in run 35381167282.

defects.title: the composite step ran under `bash -e` and died at the tool call, before recording anything
defects.effect: GitHub executes a composite `run` step as `/usr/bin/bash -e {0}`. The step's own `set -uo pipefail` looked like it was managing the shell options and was not: a script cannot turn off an `-e` the shell was invoked with by omitting it from its own `set` line. So when `actaira diff` exited 1 the step died AT THAT LINE - before the step summary, before `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, and before `actaira-exit-code.txt`, which is why DEF-117's fix could not help: the file it told the job to read was never written. The clean side exited 0 and sailed through, so the job failed in the one direction it exists to check and passed in the other. `code=0` and `|| code=$?`: a failure that is handled is a failure `-e` does not act on.
defects.found_by: running it on the runner for the first time
defects.pinned_note: Fully reproducible without a runner, which is why `tests/test_action_yml.py` exists at all: the step bodies are extracted from `action.yml` and executed under `bash -e` with a stub `actaira` on PATH. The second test named is the guard - it removes `|| code=$?` and requires the step to die and to write no file, so the first test cannot be passing under a shell that is not the one the runner uses.

defects.title: rotating a key could leave the retired one an inverted validity window, so nothing it ever signed verified again
defects.effect: `keyring.rotate` read the clock into `stamp` BEFORE calling `load_local`, and on a path with no key yet `load_local` creates one and stamps its `not_before` from its own `now_iso()`. So the stamp that `retire` writes into the retired key's `not_after` could be EARLIER than that key's `not_before`: a window running backwards, which is an empty interval. `evaluate` then rejects every moment - any instant is either before the start or after the end - so every signature that key ever made stops verifying, in a tool whose product is that an approval expires by itself rather than by accident. `now_iso` truncates to seconds, so it needed the clock to tick between two adjacent statements, which is why it survived every local run and every CI run until one interpreter out of three went red on a documentation-only commit. The fix moves one line - the stamp is read after `load_local` - so the same single stamp closes the old window and opens the new one, which is also what stops the two sides drifting into a gap. A sweep of every clock read in `attest/` found no second instance of the pattern.
defects.found_by: an intermittent failure on one interpreter
defects.pinned_note: The test forces the clock to tick between the two reads inside `rotate` and asserts BOTH invariants, because fixing either one alone breaks the other: the retired window must be ordered, and it must close exactly where the new one opens. It guards itself as well - a clock stub that returned a constant would make every assertion pass on the broken ordering, so the test checks that the clock was read twice and that the two readings differ. Verified to bite: against the code before the fix it fails with `assert '2026-09-18T19:00:01+00:00' <= '2026-09-18T19:00:00+00:00'`.

defects.title: ACT-S007 fired `critical` on `dontAsk`, which is a repository locking itself DOWN, while nine lines away the same tree refused to do that to Gemini's `plan`
defects.pinned_note: Two tests and both are needed: the first alone would pass if the clause were emptied of every value, so the second asserts ACT-S007 still fires on `bypassPermissions` and `auto`, the two modes that run what the default would have asked about. The first is parametrised over `dontAsk` AND `plan`, so it states the principle rather than the instance. Both pass a known agent version, because `bypassPermissions` without one resolves INDETERMINATE - effective before 2.1.257, not from it - and a rule never evaluates an INDETERMINATE capability; asserting it fires with no version would assert the opposite of published limit 13. The mode values come from the vendor's page, cited with its date in the test, and NOT from a grep of this tree: two greps of our own constants came back short while this was being investigated, which is why the rule is now written down. Verified to bite: putting `dontAsk` back in the clause fails `test_no_rule_fires_on_a_mode_narrower_than_the_vendors_own_default[dontAsk]`.

defects.title: a figures pattern that matched nothing was skipped in silence, so six figures declared a page they did not live on and two of them were published stale
defects.effect:
THE SHAPE FIRST, because the four regexes are the consequence and not the defect. `release_check.readme_figures_are_current` walked every (figure, page) pair the contract declares and ran the figure's pattern over the page. When the pattern matched, it compared. When it matched NOTHING, it did `continue`. So a declared figure that was not on its page was written by nobody, compared against nothing, and reported as neither wrong nor missing. `sync_readme_figures.py` had the same hole from the other side: `re.subn` returned a count of zero and the zero was added to a total nobody read. This is the same failure the whole of phase S3.1 is about - an unknown falls to the quiet answer - sitting inside the tooling that is supposed to catch it.

WHAT WAS UNGUARDED. Six pairs, found the moment the branch was made to fail. On `docs/ENGINEERING.md`: `defects`, `defect_mechanisms`, `defects_not_shipped` and `defects_by_note`. On both READMEs: `design_notes`, which declared an English and a Spanish pattern and appeared in neither page - and the bilingual check passed it because the absence was symmetric, so a third guard was silent about it too.

WHAT WAS PUBLISHED WRONG. `docs/ENGINEERING.md` said 128 defects where the ledger measured 136, and 16 distinct mechanisms where it measured 19. Directly above a sentence reading "Those four numbers are measured by `make figures` and refused by the release gate if they drift". Two of the four were right by accident: `defects_not_shipped` had not changed since somebody last typed it, and `defects_by_note` was being written by a SECOND mechanism - a regex inside `sync_readme_figures.py` that rewrote the whole ledger sentence on the ground that two of its figures "never appear on their own". That regex emitted `**136**, all fixed, **17**`, and markup between a figure and its noun is exactly what makes a lookahead stop matching. One writer produced the shape the other could not read.

THE FIX IS THE REFUSAL, NOT THE REGEXES. A page in `figure.patterns` is a DECLARATION that the figure lives there; declared and absent is a contradiction and the gate now fails on it, naming the figure, the page and the pattern. Adjusting the four lookaheads without that would have reset the trap for the fifth time, because any rewording breaks a lookahead and a broken lookahead was silent - which is precisely how these four broke. The consequences, in order: the second writer is deleted from `sync_readme_figures.py` and `defects_pinned` gets a row in the table like every other figure, so one mechanism writes each number; the ledger paragraph is rewritten with no markup between any figure and its noun and no line break inside any anchored phrase, and it now says five numbers rather than four; and `design_notes` stops declaring two pages it does not live on, through a third constructor, `measured_only`, which takes a written reason and refuses an empty one.

There is a fourth hole in the same mechanism, left standing on purpose because the refusal above covers it: `markup_split_problems` is the heuristic that was already written for this exact class - its docstring says "between a figure and the noun it counts, only whitespace" - and it reads `COUNTED_NOUNS`, which has entries for the two READMEs and none for `docs/ENGINEERING.md`. It returned an empty list for the one page whose figures had drifted. Adding nouns for that page would be a list of exceptions kept by whoever remembers to add a line; the pattern check needs nobody to remember.

A FOURTH LAYER, found when the suite ran: `tests/test_readme_parity.py::test_the_defect_counts_match_the_measured_ledger` asserted `f"**{value}**" in engineering` - it REQUIRED the bold. A test demanding the one shape that makes a figure unmatchable is a test holding the defect in place, and it is why the paragraph could not have been fixed by rewording alone. It goes through the contract's own patterns now, so "stated on this page" has a single definition and the test cannot disagree with the gate about it.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the measuring apparatus, not in the tool: `scripts/release_check.py` and `scripts/figures_contract.py` are the gate and never enter the wheel. Read with the consequence beside it, though - two figures reached a published page wrong, so `shipped_defect: false` here means the CODE did not ship, not that nothing reached a reader.
defects.pinned_note: The first breaks the PROSE and not the table, because that is the direction it happens: somebody rewords a sentence and a lookahead stops matching. It bolds the digits - `**136** defects` for `136 defects`, the exact shape the deleted sentence writer produced - and asserts the gate names the figure and says the pattern matches nothing. The second holds the door the first leaves open: a figure can satisfy the new check either by being on its page or by declaring no page, and the second is how the check gets switched off one figure at a time, so the set of figures that declare no page is asserted by name. Verified to bite: without the change to `readme_figures_are_current` the first test's tree passes the gate.

defects.title: a proxy gap test is deterministically red on Windows and green in the gate, so the platform the tree is written on is the one platform nothing checks
defects.effect:
OPEN: the entry records a measurement and a decision that has not been taken. `tests/test_proxy_completeness.py::test_every_gap_names_its_reason_and_says_what_happened[the stdio transport closed]` fails on Windows five runs out of five - not a flake - with `assert 'transport_closed' in {'result_not_recorded', 'upstream_timeout'}`: the proxy reports the stdio transport going away as an upstream timeout instead of as a closed transport. On a clean clone of the same commit in WSL, all 48 tests in that file pass, and `make all` is green at 2325 passed, 3 skipped, 23 of 23 checks. Measured on 2026-09-19 against 9d95fef, before the DEF-120 commit, so it is not a consequence of that change and nothing in this release introduced it.

WHY IT IS A DEFECT RATHER THAN A NON-EVENT. Rule 7 of CLAUDE.md puts the gate in WSL deliberately, and it is right to: a gate that runs where the developer's files are measures that machine rather than what is shipped. But `pip install actaira` works on Windows, the package declares no platform constraint, and `watch` is one of the seven commands. So either a Windows user gets a gap named `upstream_timeout` where the transport actually closed - a wrong reason in a document whose whole product is that a gap names its cause - or the behaviour is fine and the test's timing assumption is not portable. WHICH OF THE TWO IT IS HAS NOT BEEN ESTABLISHED, and that is why `shipped_defect` is true: the conservative reading is the one that does not flatter the count, which is this ledger's own rule.

THE DECISION, due before phase L and not in S3.1. Either the test is platform-specific and is skipped on Windows WITH ITS REASON WRITTEN - in which case the reason has to say what Windows does differently, not merely that it differs - or the function does not run on Windows and that is a PUBLISHED LIMIT, in the README and in the limits list, not a footnote. What is not available is leaving it as it is: the gate's silence about Windows is by design, and a defect that hides inside a designed silence is the shape this repository files defects about.

AND A NOTE THE LEDGER OWES ITSELF. This is entry 122 and the first one that carries `fixed: false`. Until it, `docs/ENGINEERING.md` said "all fixed" - hand-written prose that `sync_readme_figures.py` captured and re-emitted without ever checking it, which meant the ledger could only ever hold defects that were already closed. A ledger that admits only fixed defects is not a ledger, it is a list of achievements. That DEF-121 is the first open one of 122 is not an anomaly: it is the first time the ledger did its whole job. `fixed` is now required on every entry, with no default, and `still_open` is measured from it and published - the ledger's own anti-flattery rule turned on the ledger. The backfill takes the previous claim at its word: the other 121 are marked fixed because "all fixed" stood as a published claim until now, and from here the state is per entry rather than a global adjective.

RESOLVED, AND NOT AS EITHER OF THE TWO BRANCHES ALONE. `watch` WORKS on Windows: the healthy path is indistinguishable from Linux's - exit 0, capture level L1, the tool call observed, the trace and its digest written, four records ending in `end`. So this is not a defect in `watch`, and "the function does not run on Windows" is false.

THE ROOT CAUSE, three ways of a child ending its output, parent reading the pipe, measured 2026-09-19: the child EXITS - Windows 0.3s, Linux 0.0s; the child closes fd 1 and STAYS ALIVE - Linux 0.0s, WINDOWS NEVER (still blocked past 6s); the child closes fd 1 and exits a second later - Windows 2.1s, Linux 0.0s. Pipes work. The one signal Windows does not deliver is a LIVE writer closing its end, which is exactly and only what `transport_closed` is about. So it is not the test's timing assumption either: the fake server does what a real server would do and the platform does not report it.

BOTH BRANCHES, because the dilemma was false. The scenario is skipped on Windows AND the fact is published as limit 15, in both READMEs, in `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` under a new Platforms section, and in CLAUDE.md. The anchor is the LIMIT and not the skip: a skipped test is the absence of a check and an absence holds nothing in place. The pin asserts the limit is published and that the skip's reason is the same sentence - work rule 10 on its first day, since two statements about one property of Windows either share their definition or cancel, which is DEF-122 in a new place. The sentence lives once, as `WINDOWS_TRANSPORT_CLOSED_LIMIT` in `proxy/stdio.py`, and the skip prints it.

`end_not_recorded` WAS ASKED ABOUT SEPARATELY AND IS NOT A SECOND DEFECT. End to end on Windows the trace also lost the session end, and the question was whether that is a close path that never writes. It is not. With a client more patient than the proxy's 30s deadline, the same Windows run records four lines ending in `end`, with the gap present (as `upstream_timeout`) and `end_not_recorded` gone. And the same shape reproduces IN WSL with a different trigger: a live, silent server and a client that gives up at 12s produces two records and `end_not_recorded` there too. It is what any killed proxy reports, on any platform, and it is true - a process that is killed cannot write its close record, and the trace saying so is the tool being honest. On Windows it is downstream of the missing EOF: no EOF means the proxy waits its full deadline, which puts every client less patient than 30s into the kill path. It is named inside limit 15 as the practical consequence, and explicitly as NOT platform-specific.
defects.found_by: running the gate on the development machine
defects.pinned_note: Pinned on the LIMIT, not on the skip, because a skipped test anchors nothing. The test asserts the published sentence is the constant the skip prints, in `README.md` and in `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md`, comparing with whitespace and blockquote markers normalised so that line wrapping is allowed to differ and words are not. It also asserts the two READMEs state the same NUMBER of limits and that both carry 15 and 16 by number - counting alone would pass if the Spanish page lost the limit and the English one lost it too, which is the symmetric-absence error DEF-122 found in the `design_notes` parity check. Verified to bite: rewording the README's copy from "cannot be told apart" to "cannot be distinguished" fails the test.

defects.title: the Action's documented path never worked: `--sarif` landed after the `--`, so `diff` got four refs and exited 2 on every pull request that used it
defects.effect:
THE DEFECT. `action.yml` built the tool's arguments as `set -- --repo . -- "$base" "$head"` and then called `actaira diff "$@" --sarif "$ACTAIRA_SARIF"`. The `--` ends option parsing, so `--sarif` and its path arrived as two more POSITIONALS: `diff` received four refs where it takes two, printed `diff wants two refs, oldest first, or --from-dir and --to-dir`, and exited 2 - EXIT_USAGE. Reproducible in one line: `actaira --lang en diff --repo . -- <base> <head> --sarif out.sarif`.

WHAT THAT MEANT. The refs branch is the ONLY path the documentation describes: `on: pull_request` with no inputs, base and head taken from the event. So the published Action had never worked for the way it tells people to use it. Not intermittently - always, and since it was written. Had this reached PyPI and the Marketplace, every person who installed it as the README says would have seen a usage error on their first pull request.

HOW IT SURVIVED, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH READING. CI's `action` job is named "the published Action, used the way a stranger would" and it passes `from-dir`/`to-dir`. That branch builds an argv with NO `--` in it, so `--sarif` parsed correctly and the job was green. The job's own comment argued that `from-dir` exists so that a job testing the Action would not end up testing a repository it built - a good-sounding argument for exercising the one shape a stranger never writes. A stranger does not pass `from-dir`. `tests/test_action_yml.py` was green for the same reason from the other side: its stub was `#!/bin/sh ... exit N`, which accepts any argv at all, so every assertion about exit codes passing through was made over a call the tool would have refused.

FOUND BY THREE REAL PULL REQUESTS in point 10 of phase S3, on marcosmatalab/plazum, /MACE and /samegold. All three red, all three exit 2, all three the same message. The point was designed as a formality and it is what stopped the launch.

THE FIX IS THREE THINGS, because one of them alone would leave it able to come back. First, every option now goes into `$@` BEFORE the `--` and nothing is appended after `"$@"` at the call site; the `--` stays, because it is well argued and protects against a branch whose name starts with a dash. Second, the test stops stubbing the judgement: the stub RECORDS its argv and the REAL CLI decides, over real inputs - a git repository with two commits for the refs branch, two directories for the other - so there is one definition of "an argv `diff` accepts" and it is the user's. Third, CI's `action` job now exercises the refs branch as well, over two commits it makes in its own checkout, which is gate point 9 of phase S3 redone: that point was signed off on the same false premise as point 10 and falls with it.

Phase S3 loses two gate points and does not close.
defects.found_by: running it on the runner for the first time
defects.pinned_note: Parametrised over both branches, `dirs` and `refs`, because only one of them had ever been exercised anywhere and the one nobody ran is the one that was broken. The stub is pure shell and writes its arguments one per line; the real `cli.main` is then handed exactly those arguments, in the directory the step ran in, and the assertion is that it does not come back EXIT_USAGE. Verified to bite: putting `--sarif` back after `"$@"` fails `...[refs]` with the tool's own message on stderr and leaves `...[dirs]` green, which is precisely the asymmetry that hid the defect.

defects.title: the fix for DEF-123 moved a closing quote into a later step, so CI died on unparseable shell before reaching the branch that commit existed to add
defects.effect:
THE DEFECT. The commit that fixed DEF-123 added three steps to the `action` job of `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, and inserted them ABOVE the line that closed a `python -c "` string. The closing quote ended up at the foot of the file, inside a LATER step's `run:` block. Two steps were then unparseable shell: the one that lost its quote and the one that inherited it. The runner said `unexpected EOF while looking for matching '"'` and the job exited 2 at `the exit codes are the ones the contract publishes`.

WHAT THAT MEANT. The three steps the commit existed to add are the ones AFTER the broken one, so they were skipped. DEF-123's fix - the `base`/`head` branch, the path the documentation tells people to use - still had not run on a runner once. A commit whose whole argument was `this path has never been exercised` shipped without exercising it, and said so in its own message.

HOW IT SURVIVED, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH READING. The YAML stayed valid, so every reader that reads YAML stayed happy: `zizmor --persona=auditor` passed, `make all` passed, the suite passed. `tests/test_action_yml.py` extracts the `run:` bodies of `action.yml` and EXECUTES them - it exists because of DEF-116, DEF-117 and DEF-118, three defects in that same seam - and it does not read `.github/workflows/` at all. So the repository had a check built precisely for shell-embedded-in-YAML, and its green covered one of the two files that have that shape. Work rule 12 again, the sixth instance: a check that looks at the thing next to the thing, passes, and is read as having looked at both.

FOUND BY the first CI run of the push that published it, which is also the only machine that could have found it: nothing on a laptop parsed that shell.

THE FIX IS TWO THINGS. The quote goes back to the step it belongs to. And `tests/test_workflow_shell.py` hands every piece of shell this repository embeds in a file that is not a shell script to `bash -n`: the `run:` bodies of every workflow under `.github/workflows/`, of `action.yml` (twice covered on purpose - the cheap check and the executing one), and the `RUN` instructions of the `Dockerfile`. The published kits under `.launch/` carry no `run:` and the sweep ASSERTS that rather than assuming it, so the day one grows a `run:` the sweep fails instead of skipping it. The extractor is the one `test_action_yml.py` already had, imported rather than copied - work rule 10 - and writing this found two more holes in it: it read only `run: |`, which would have left seven of `ci.yml`'s sixteen blocks unread, and it keyed by step label, which silently DROPPED every unnamed step after the first. Both were the same disease as the defect itself.

defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the gate, not in the tool: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is the integration definition and never enters the wheel. Read with the consequence beside it, though - what it broke was the run that would have demonstrated the SHIPPED fix of DEF-123, so a defect outside the package left a defect inside it unverified for as long as it stood.
defects.pinned_note: Verified to bite against the defect as published rather than against a reconstruction: the sweep run over `ci.yml` at 487eae9 reports both broken steps with the runner's own message, `unexpected EOF while looking for matching '"'`. `test_the_sweep_would_notice_an_unterminated_quote` is the twin required by work rule 9 and plants the defect in the shape it happened - a step inserted between a `python -c "` and the line that closed it - demanding two failures from the same function the real sweep calls, not from a private copy. `test_the_sweep_found_the_files_and_the_blocks_it_thinks_it_did` is the work rule 11 guard: it pins the block counts (16 in `ci.yml`, 4 in `action.yml`, 2 `RUN` in the `Dockerfile`) so an extractor that quietly stopped matching cannot make the sweep pass over nothing.
